## Introduction {#sec-introduction}

The race to build artificial intelligence infrastructure commits an unusually large and concentrated pool of capital: combined 2026 capital expenditure by the four largest compute providers was guided to roughly \$720--745 billion in mid-2026, up from \$660--690 billion at the start of the year,^[Sources: Alphabet Q2 2026 earnings release (SEC EDGAR, exhibit 99.1, July 22, 2026); Meta Q2 2026 earnings release (July 29, 2026); Amazon and Microsoft Q2 2026 earnings calls (July 29--30, 2026), as reported by CNBC and CFO Dive.] OpenAI's Stargate joint venture targets up to \$500 billion in U.S. AI infrastructure through 2029,^[\url{https://openai.com/index/announcing-the-stargate-project/}.] and Anthropic's forward compute commitments reportedly exceed \$500 billion, most of them non-cancellable.^[Reuters, reporting on Anthropic's IPO prospectus, September 28, 2026.] These investments are largely irreversible, and the uncertainty that drives them, whether and when AI capabilities reach a transformative threshold, is unresolved. This paper asks how a firm should time, size, and allocate an irreversible capacity investment when the return to that capacity depends on a regime change whose arrival is uncertain and whose competitive consequences depend on how the capacity was used beforehand.

The allocation margin is what makes the problem distinctive. A frontier AI laboratory produces intelligence by combining two forms of compute drawn from the same scarce hardware: *training compute*, which optimizes a neural network's parameters on massive datasets and yields a model whose quality scales as a power law of compute invested [@kaplan2020scaling; @altman2025observations], and *inference compute*, which runs the trained model to serve predictions and generate revenue. The same asset can either produce revenue now or build the capability that determines the firm's position in a future that may not arrive, and capacity devoted to training earns nothing until then while its operating cost is paid from the start. The split therefore sets both what the firm is worth if that future arrives and how far demand can fall before the firm stops operating, so the option to grow and the risk of failure run through a single decision.

Firms must commit this capital under widely different beliefs about the same event, Artificial General Intelligence (AGI): a step change in model capability sufficient to automate a broad range of cognitive tasks and generate sustained, qualitatively higher demand for compute [@amodei2024machines]. Executive forecasts of its arrival run from "superintelligence in a few thousand days" [@altman2024intelligence] and 2026--2027 [@amodei2024machines] to "not with current architectures."^[PYMNTS, "Meta: Large Language Models Will Not Get to Human-Level Intelligence," 2025.]

I develop a model in which a firm chooses when to invest, how much capacity to install, and what fraction $\phi$ to devote to training versus inference, facing regime-switching demand [@guo2005investment], a rival in a duopoly entry game [@grenadier2002option; @huisman2015strategic], endogenous default [@leland1994corporate], and diminishing returns to capacity, with the curvature parameter motivated by empirical scaling laws [@kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022training]. In regime $L$, the current low-demand regime, revenue depends on inference capacity through a Tullock contest; in regime $H$, the post-AGI regime, it depends on training compute. A firm may invest before or after the switch. The allocation and the post-switch policy are in closed form; the pre-switch policy and the duopoly equilibrium are numerical.

The paper makes three contributions. First, at the baseline calibration competition, not the single firm's own option, brings investment forward of the switch. A single firm that can choose its scale when the switch arrives waits for it, because investing earlier buys only pre-switch inference revenue while the post-switch prize is obtained at least as cheaply by waiting. In the duopoly one firm invests before the switch at every arrival rate examined (Proposition 3). The force at work is the race that follows the switch, not a race before it: a firm that waits enters a post-switch race in which the rent from leading is competed away. At the date of first investment following is the better role, so the pre-switch game has a second-mover advantage, and the demand level at which leading and following are worth the same is an upper bound on that date. Against a single firm whose post-switch scale is precommitted, first investment comes at a demand level $64\%$ lower at baseline. The optimal training fraction has a closed form that rises with the arrival rate of the switch and does not depend on scale (Proposition 1). Competitive position moves the leader's allocation only modestly at baseline, where its training fraction lies $3.1\%$ below the single firm's; a follower that enters after the switch trains with all its capacity. The equilibrium is verified numerically on a grid: uniqueness is not shown, the symmetric equilibrium in mixed strategies is not solved, and the assignment of roles is a selection.

Second, I identify *faith-based survival*, a channel from beliefs to solvency that runs through the allocation. Installed capacity carries a perpetual operating cost, so the firm's owners stop operating at a shutdown boundary that exists without any debt and that leverage shifts. When the firm trains enough, a higher arrival rate lowers that boundary. I characterize the net threshold on the training fraction in closed form for a single-boundary reduction of the default problem (Proposition 2), and the optimal allocation exceeds it for arrival rates above about $0.034$ at baseline. At a fixed belief the boundary is U-shaped in the training fraction, so training beyond the optimum raises it. The continuation value is lost in default and recovery is at most $5\%$ of the claim at the model's policies, so credit risk there is the risk of reaching the boundary (@sec-valuation).

Third, I quantify *Dario's dilemma*, the loss a firm incurs by investing on a belief about the AGI arrival rate $\lambda$ that differs from its true value (Numerical Finding 1). Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei describes the optimistic side: "I could buy \$1 trillion of compute that starts at the end of 2027... there's no hedge on Earth that could stop me from going bankrupt" [@amodei2026dwarkesh]. The training allocation is the largest component of the loss on both sides. For a single firm with precommitted post-switch scale, with values measured at half the informed firm's trigger, investing as though $\lambda = 0.02$ when the true rate is $0.10$ costs $32\%$ of firm value, against $1.3\%$ for investing as though $\lambda = 0.18$, an error of the same size in $\lambda$. The comparison depends on how the two errors are matched. For equal proportional errors the pessimistic error still costs more, by a smaller factor ($32\%$ against $13\%$ at a factor of five, $\lambda = 0.02$ and $0.50$), and for equal errors in the expected time to the switch the two cost about the same. The pessimistic firm invests early and small, not late, with too little training. Tail risk arises without debt, and leverage adds to it. The far optimist ($\lambda = 0.50$) reaches its shutdown boundary within five years with probability $1.8\%$ without any debt, about eleven times the informed firm's $0.16\%$ (upper bounds that ignore the switch). In the duopoly a mistaken leader loses more on both sides. A stylized calibration maps the training allocations assigned to four AI lab archetypes into implied beliefs (@sec-calibration); because the allocations are assigned, the exercise is not evidence that beliefs explain differences across firms.

@sec-model presents the model and Propositions 1 to 3, @sec-calibration the stylized calibration, and @sec-valuation the quantitative implications. @sec-discussion considers testable predictions, policy implications, and limitations, and @sec-conclusion concludes. The Internet Appendix collects the proofs, numerical verification methods, calibration sources, robustness exercises, and supporting exhibits.
